slides.transcript: [gentle music] Welcome to the world of chiplets, a breakthrough in semiconductor design that enhances scalability, performance, and cost efficiency. For decades, Moore's Law has driven chip advancements, doubling transistor counts every two years. However, as chips become larger and more complex, they face manufacturing limits, lower yields, and increased costs. Expanding chip size or increasing transistor density has become increasingly difficult. A new approach is needed, one that enables scalability, flexibility, and cost savings. Instead of a single massive chip, chiplets allow designers to break complex systems into smaller specialized modules. These chiplets can be manufactured separately and assembled into a high-performance package. Package sizes can go beyond the reticle limit. Moreover, package size and wiring density are projected to grow rapidly, providing headroom for growth and investment protection. This modular approach offers significant advantages, lower manufacturing costs, improved yields, and the flexibility to reuse as well as mix and match chiplets for different applications. However, there are also challenges to consider. Chiplet-based systems can incur higher package costs and higher testing costs compared to traditional monolithic designs. Additionally, the interoperability challenge, especially when integrating chiplets from different vendors. How do chiplets connect? Packaging plays a critical role. Different methods like 2D, 2.5D, and 3D stacking enable efficient chiplet integration depending on the needs. Leading companies like Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA have already adopted chiplet-based architectures with applications expanding into AI, cloud computing, and consumer electronics. Industry analysts agree the market for chiplet ecosystems is growing at a rapid rate with widespread adoption across enterprise and compute, communications, industrial, consumer electronics, and automotive industries. In this series of courses, we'll explore the technology and challenges to be solved in the areas of chiplet architectures, packaging technologies, die-to-die interfaces, cost structures, and the growing open chiplet economy. Are you ready to dive in? Let's explore the world of chiplets and unlock the future of semiconductor innovation. [gentle music]

slides.transcript: [gentle music] Chiplets are revolutionizing semiconductor design by enabling flexible modular architectures that improve scalability, performance, and cost efficiency. For decades, semiconductor advancements relied on monolithic chips, single large integrated circuits packed with billions of transistors. However, as computing demands grow, these chips are approaching physical and economic limitations. Higher complexity leads to increased power consumption, manufacturing defects, and lower yields. The industry now requires a more adaptable and scalable approach to chip design. Chiplets provide an alternative approach by breaking down a larger chip into smaller modular components. These chiplets can be manufactured separately and assembled together in a package. Heterogeneous integration builds on this concept by allowing chiplets from different process nodes, functions, or even different manufacturers to work together seamlessly. This approach enables optimization. Compute chips can be built on leading-edge nodes, while analog and memory components can use mature, cost-effective nodes. There are multiple methods for integrating chiplets, including 2D, 2.5D, and 3D stacking, each offering trade-offs in performance, power, and cost. Technological advances make it possible to go both horizontal and vertical. With two-dimensional packages, multiple dies can be mounted on a package substrate that connects them. In 2.5D, packaging enables dies to be mounted on silicon interposer and interconnected with finer metal wires. In 3D, multiple dies can be stacked or mounted on top of other dies, enabling even more and shorter connections between the dies. In many cases, 2D, 2.5D, and 3D may be mixed in the same package, giving more flexibility for heterogeneous integration. With chiplet-based silicon design, common functions like core, cache, memory, and I/O can be sliced into modular dies and packaged together to form a larger system. Today, silicon area can be 1700 millimeters squared, nearly double the 850 millimeter squared size of monolithic dies. And what's more, package sizes are projected to double in the next few years, opening up significant growth opportunities. [gentle music]

slides.transcript: [upbeat music] Welcome. In this video lesson, we're diving into a fundamental concept, heterogeneous versus homogeneous disaggregation. These approaches define how large system on chips, or SoCs, are broken down and reassembled using chiplets. As we push the limits of monolithic SoCs, disaggregation emerges as a powerful solution. It allows smaller modular chiplets to be assembled into a single package, enhancing yield, cost efficiency, flexibility, and crucially, improving SWaP, size, weight, and power. Homogeneous disaggregation means breaking down a large SoC into smaller chiplets that use the same process node. Each chiplet retains the same function as part of the original design, optimizing silicon utilization, and improving yield due to smaller die sizes. Heterogeneous disaggregation, on the other hand, takes this concept further. Instead of keeping everything in the same process node, we optimize functional blocks into different nodes. This allows, for example, logic to be built in an advanced node while analog and I/O remain on mature, cost-effective nodes. A real-world example of heterogeneous integration is high bandwidth memory, or HBM, which is built in an advanced DRAM process node and stacks memory on top of a base logic die using 3D integration techniques. The key advantages of homogeneous disaggregation include cost savings due to higher yield or building a smaller unit die, such as a CPU core, that can be repeated several times to scale performance. Heterogeneous disaggregation, meanwhile, unlocks greater efficiency by tailoring each function to the most suitable process node. As chips in older process nodes are faster to design and cheaper to build, this means lower cost and faster time to market. Additionally, an optimized process node can also improve performance. In summary, both approaches serve different needs. Homogeneous disaggregation is about efficiency and yield, while heterogeneous disaggregation maximizes performance and cost savings by integrating optimized functional blocks. This is just the beginning of what's possible with chiplet architectures. Later in this course, we'll explore how package-level aggregation compares to PCB-based integration. [upbeat music]

slides.transcript: [upbeat music] In past courses, you learned a bit about packaging chiplets into a system. But did you know that integrating multiple chips, often from different process technologies, has been practiced for decades? Standard wire bond and flip chip on substrate technologies, known as 2D packaging, are commonly employed to combine disparate technologies in a single package for performance or form factor considerations. The cost incurred in these cases is minimal, and in some instances, it may even be lower than the cost of individually packaging each die. Multi-chip packaging serves multiple purposes, minimizing interface losses, separating different technologies such as logic and analog, and increasing product value through added functionality. The reasons for multi-chip packaging also applies to chiplets. Remember, chiplets are a product strategy enabled by packaging. By creating a portfolio of reusable and interchangeable blocks, chiplets allow products to be brought to market faster with lower R&D costs. The choice of packaging impacts factors like power efficiency, interconnect density, and manufacturing complexity. Chiplet packaging also unlocks new opportunities, such as optimizing silicon technology nodes for specific functionalities, bridging products for socket security before product optimization, and enabling higher value systems with increased margin. A chiplet product packaging platform must meet performance and cost requirements while offering scalability across product tiers and generations. Now that we've explored the fundamentals of chiplet packaging, let's examine a key aspect of packaging, chip-to-chip interface requirements. High performance chiplet integration depends on advanced interconnect technologies. Let's dive in. [upbeat music]

slides.transcript: [upbeat music] Let's now look at different options for packaging chiplet technologies. The evolution of packaging has enabled new levels of integration, performance, and scalability in modern semiconductor design. Chiplet packaging is defined largely on the first connection between the chip and the base on which it sits, the interposer or substrate. This first connection affects data transfer speeds, signal integrity, chip size, and overall cost. Semiconductor packaging varies from basic single chip designs to complex 3D stacking with intermediate solutions using bridges or interposers. First, 2D packaging places chiplets side by side with bridged interconnects on organic substrate or a fan-out redistribution layer. Such packaging methods are ideal for cost-sensitive applications like mobile and IoT driven by digital or analog disaggregation. Higher cost 2.5D and 3D packaging suits high-performance data center and automotive compute. However, these cost models may shift as technology and industry capacity evolve. 2.5D packaging builds on this by introducing a silicon interposer with through-silicon vias or TSVs. A TSV is a vertical electrical connection that passes through a silicon wafer. It enables high density interconnects for 2.5D and 3D packaging of integrated circuits, allowing for shorter wiring and improved performance. Next, 2.5D packaging introduces a passive TSV interposer, whereas 3D packaging uses an active TSV interposer and hybrid bonding. 2.5D is like arranging chiplets on a special connecting platform. 3D is like stacking chiplets on top of each other. 3D provides the best performance, but at a higher cost, while 2.5D offers a good balance between performance and cost. Finally, in 3D packaging, hybrid bonding offers the highest interconnect density by combining dielectric and metal bonding at the wafer level. This technique enables extremely small bump pitches, improving signal integrity and reducing power consumption. Chiplet packaging technologies continue to evolve, driving the next generation of computing. Let's continue our journey into the future of chiplet packaging. [upbeat music]

slides.transcript: [gentle music] Let's explore die-to-die interface metrics and why understanding them is crucial, the key metrics that define their performance, and how they impact chiplet-based systems. Let's start with the basics. Die-to-die, or D2D, interfaces are essential for communication between chiplets within a package. Unlike traditional chip-to-chip connections, they have shorter reach and consume significantly less power. They are often 10 times more efficient than standard chip-to-chip interconnects like SPI or LVDS. These interfaces are crucial in modular semiconductor design, where multiple chiplets from different vendors must work together seamlessly. Standardization plays a key role in ensuring interoperability and scalability. So how do we compare different die-to-die interfaces? There are four primary metrics: energy consumption, latency, bandwidth density, and packaging requirements. Energy consumption tells us how much energy is needed to transport data across the interface. It's measured in picojoules per bit. Lower values mean more energy-efficient communication. For example, if an interface operates at one picojoules per bit while transferring one terabit per second, it would consume one watt of power. Latency measures the time delay in data transmission, typically in nanoseconds or clock cycles. It can be strongly influenced by error correction. High-latency interfaces can slow down system performance, making this a critical factor for real-time applications. Bandwidth density measures how much bandwidth can be packed into a given space, often measured in gigabits per second per millimeter of die edge. A higher value allows for more data throughput without increasing the physical footprint. Packaging requirements are defined by bump pitch, which determines how densely interconnects can be packed on the die. A bump pitch over 110 microns supports standard laminate packaging, while smaller pitches less than 110 microns require advanced packaging solutions. Next, we'll look at the three major chiplet interfaces in use today: extra short reach, or XSR; ultra short reach, or USR; bunch of wires and universal chiplet interconnect express, or UCIe. Each has its trade-offs measured in the metrics you just learned of, specifically in terms of bandwidth, power efficiency, and packaging capability. With continuous advancements, standardization efforts, and innovative packaging solutions, die-to-die interfaces are evolving rapidly. Understanding these metrics helps optimize chiplet-based architectures for performance, cost, and efficiency. [gentle music]

slides.transcript: [light music] Testing is a crucial part of chiplet-based systems, ensuring quality, reliability, and cost efficiency at every stage of the manufacturing process. Advanced packaging has resulted in increased challenges in chiplet testability. Chiplet testing happens at multiple levels: wafer level, die level, and whole system package level. Each step is designed to detect defects, optimize yield, and improve long-term reliability of the product with the lowest escape rate. First, substrate testing ensures that the foundation for chiplet integration is defect-free. This is done by using flying probe tests to detect open circuits and shorts in interconnects. Next, wafer level sorting and testing by automatic equipment is performed before the wafer is diced into individual chiplets. This includes probe tests, burn-in tests, and parametric analysis to measure electrical characteristics. After dicing, chiplets undergo die level testing. This includes scan tests and functional tests to identify known good dies, or KGDs, that are free of defects before they are packaged. Once assembled into multi-chip modules and then packages, chiplet systems undergo package level testing and fault isolation. This ensures that all chiplets are correctly connected, functional, and performing as expected. System level testing is the final step, validating the entire assembled product in real world conditions. This includes thermal, power, and functional stress tests. Design for testability, or DFT techniques, such as scan chains, boundary scan, and built-in self-test or BIST, help streamline testing and improve fault detection. Standardized testing protocols from IEEE and JEDEC, such as IEEE 1149.x for boundary scan and IEEE 1838 for 3D integrated circuits or ICs, ensure interoperability and test reliability. Chiplet testing can significantly reduce manufacturing costs as it ensures that a broken chiplet or package does not get assembled in a larger system where it leads to throwing out the entire assembly and many good subcomponents with it. Testing ensures the long-term reliability of semiconductor products. In this course, we will explore chiplet testing methodologies, industry standards, and best practices for ensuring high-quality chiplet-based systems. Let's continue our journey into the future of chiplet manufacturing and testing. [light music]

slides.transcript: [upbeat music] Welcome. In this module, we'll explore how chiplet technology provides a yield advantage, a design cost advantage, and accelerates time to market, all of which contribute to a more cost-effective and scalable semiconductor industry. Let's start with yield advantage. In traditional monolithic chip designs, larger dies have lower yields because any defect in the wafer could result in a faulty chip. But with chiplets, the die sizes are smaller, which increases the number of functional dies per wafer and improves yield. This leads to lower overall manufacturing costs. Next, we have the design cost advantage. Advanced semiconductor nodes are expensive, and not all components of a system benefit equally from cutting-edge technology. Chiplets allow manufacturers to use the optimal process for each function. For example, logic can be fabricated at the latest nodes, while analog and memory functions remain in older, more cost-effective nodes. This leads us to another key benefit, faster time to market. By reusing pre-designed chiplets, companies can reduce development time and avoid the risks of designing an entire chip from scratch. Whether using in-house chiplets or those from third parties, such as from the marketplace in OCP's, Open Chiplet Economy, businesses can accelerate product launches and gain a competitive edge. Of course, these benefits come with some trade-offs. While chiplet architectures reduce die costs, they can increase packaging and testing costs. However, the overall balance still favors cost savings, especially in scenarios where chiplets enable customization and scalability. The chiplet model is revolutionizing semiconductor economics. Whether it's better yield, optimized design costs, or a faster time to market, the financial benefits are clear. slides.transcript: [upbeat music] Standardized integration workflows are key to ensuring chiplets from different vendors can be seamlessly integrated into a single system. Chiplet integration requires a structured process to manage design, verification, packaging, and testing. Without standardization, interoperability becomes a major challenge. The chiplet product development workflow is typically divided into four phases: planning and prototyping, design implementation, verification and signoff, and final manufacturing. In the planning phase, engineers define system architecture and ensure compatibility between chiplets, packaging, and interconnect standards. Next, during the design implementation phase, chip designers design chiplets according to the specifications outlined in the planning phase. For existing chiplets from other vendors, they can use standardized data exchange formats such as JEDEC JESD30 or CDXML to ensure consistency across tools and vendors. Power, signal integrity, and thermal models are critical for ensuring chiplets function correctly within the package. Standardized formats help simplify integration and analysis. The verification and signoff phase ensures all components meet performance and reliability standards. This includes functional simulation, die-to-die signal verification, and compliance testing. During manufacturing, chiplets are tested at multiple levels from wafer level to system level. Interoperability standards like UCIe and Bunch of Wires, or BoW, define how chiplets communicate, making it possible for components from different vendors to work together. A well-defined integration workflow ensures higher efficiency, reduced development time, and greater market adoption for chiplet-based designs. In this course, we explored the critical aspects of integration workflow standards, including data exchange formats, verification processes, and best practices. [upbeat music]

slides.transcript: [gentle music] A marketplace of chiplets presents opportunities and challenges. In previous modules, you've learned of opportunities like reusing proven chiplets, mixing different process nodes, and reducing development time and costs, as well as challenges such as the need for high-speed die-to-die interfaces, interoperability between different vendors' chiplets, and the complexities and costs associated with advanced packaging and testability. A marketplace of chiplets is based on the emerging chiplet paradigm shift away from traditional monolithic chip design, where a single complex chip serves all functions, toward a more flexible mix-and-match approach. In this course, we'll look at opportunities and challenges in turn and what role the marketplace is serving. Let's start with the opportunities. First, chiplets enable cost efficiency. Companies can design and manufacture smaller, specialized components rather than expensive, large-scale chips, reducing production costs and risks. This creates more marketplace diversity by creating a role for the chiplet creator and a role for the assembler, as well as other nuanced roles in between and downstream. This modularity also accelerates innovation, as firms can swap or upgrade individual chiplets, such as for AI memory or I/O, without redesigning an entire system on chip, or SoC. This means that a company could pair a high-performance CPU chiplet with a tailored GPU chiplet to meet specific needs, fostering rapid prototyping and deployment. Additionally, a marketplace democratizes access, allowing smaller players to compete by sourcing chiplets rather than designing all chiplets on their own, a significant advantage amid soaring fabrication costs, where, for example, TSMC's advanced nodes cost millions to tape out in. Finally, sustainability also benefits, as reusable chiplets reduce waste compared to discarding entire SoCs. Now let's turn to challenges. This model introduces complexity. Interoperability is a major hurdle. Chiplets from different vendors must communicate seamlessly, requiring standardized interfaces, as discussed in module four. Without robust standards, integration could falter, leading to performance bottlenecks or incompatibility. Quality control poses another issue. A single defective chiplet could compromise an entire system. Yet testing modular components across a supply chain is trickier than vetting a monolithic chip. Intellectual property and security risks are also a concern. Vendors may hesitate to share proprietary designs, and combining chiplets could expose vulnerabilities if not tightly coordinated. Finally, the marketplace demands a mature ecosystem, including reliable suppliers, clear pricing, and trust, which is still developing. In a sense, a chiplet marketplace promises innovation and accessibility but hinges on solving technical, logistical, and economic challenges to truly disrupt the semiconductor landscape. In the OCP community, The Open Chiplet Economy Project is committed to facilitating that work, and the OCP's multi-vendor open marketplace has a dedicated section for chiplets, too, including everything from technical and business tools and components to design, assemble, test, and package chiplets. [gentle music]

slides.transcript: [gentle music] The Open Compute Project is leading the way in chiplet collaboration, creating an open marketplace where vendors, designers, and manufacturers can cooperate and share. OCP's marketplace has a dedicated area for chiplets open to all solution providers. Today, it covers products and technologies for assembly and test, specifications, CDXML, cost modeling, design services, EDA, manufacturing and packaging, power components, and chiplets and IP blocks themselves. Through an open marketplace, companies can source pre-validated chiplets, reducing design complexity. And by helping to standardize interfaces and improve interoperability, the OCP open chiplet economy lowers development barriers, reduces costs, and accelerates time to market for new chiplet-based products. The OCP Experience Centers showcase real-world applications of OCP contributions. The primary focus of any OCP Experience Center is to accelerate open innovation and facilitate the widespread adoption of OCP recognized equipment. These centers are a cornerstone in OCP strategy to penetrate emerging markets, and they complement the OCP Ready product recognition and OCP Safe programs. The target audience for these centers includes adopters and channel partners seeking firsthand experience with OCP hardware. OCP Experience Centers can provide in-person or virtual access designed to provide proof points around OCP solutions, gaining a deeper understanding of the benefits offered by OCP recognized equipment. When it comes to chiplets, Lawrence Berkeley National Lab hosts the OCP Experience Center dedicated to the open chiplet economy. It features technology demonstrations showcasing products and prototypes from different sectors of the emerging chiplet market, impacting the development of specialized ASICs for HPC. These demonstrations will include chiplets, chiplet-based products, IP, workflow and manufacturing innovations, as well as tools that help designers integrate chiplets into ASICs. The Berkeley Lab is also hosting periodic workshops to showcase these demonstrations and bring together industry leaders to discuss the future of chiplet technology. OCP is providing the tools and resources needed to enable the future of chiplets, but real transformation happens when individuals like you get involved. Let's see how you can contribute to shaping the future of chiplets. [gentle music]

lms_catalog.short_description: Explore chiplet architecture, packaging, interfaces, testing, economics, and the standards enabling an open chiplet ecosystem.
lms_catalog.overview: This series connects the business case for chiplets with the engineering decisions needed to build viable systems. Explore architecture, packaging, communication, test, cost, and interoperability, then examine supplier qualification and opportunities to contribute to the Open Chiplet Economy. Narrated explanations, technical videos, and knowledge checks connect component choices to complete system outcomes.

modules.summary: Explore the motivations for chiplets, including process selection, yield, reuse, and product flexibility. Understand how open interfaces, standards, and integration tools support the ecosystem.
Compare aggregation and disaggregation, evaluate partition boundaries, and identify the traffic, latency, and interface overhead that must be considered during architectural planning.
Compare substrates, fan-out, bridges, interposers, and hybrid bonding. Connect packaging choices to interconnect density, manufacturing yield, test access, power delivery, and thermal design.
Distinguish physical signaling, link behavior, and protocol meaning. Compare interface metrics and examine how standards, versions, profiles, and implementation evidence affect compatibility.
Examine testing at die, package, and system stages. Explore controllability, observability, test access, and the information suppliers and integrators need for coverage and diagnosis.
Evaluate engineering investment and recurring production costs. Consider yield, packaging, assembly, screening, reuse, and supply assumptions when comparing cost per shipped good system.
Explore models, exchange formats, integration workflows, and the 3DK framework. Understand the roles of assembly, material, and test design kits in supporting interoperability.

Follow a chiplet from catalog discovery to system qualification. Examine the technical collateral, support, supply commitments, and lifecycle responsibilities needed for successful procurement and integration.

Examine emerging ecosystem directions, distinguish published contributions from proposals, and identify practical ways to participate. Bring architectural, commercial, and trust considerations into a system decision brief.
